paper_title: BiSAT: Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization for Speech Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Speech language models (LMs) generate speech as sequences of discrete tokens, requiring tokenizers that preserve both acoustic detail and linguistic content at a low bitrate. Semanticenhanced tokenizers may discard acoustic detail, whereas acousticoriented tokenizers retain acoustic variation that hinders language modeling. Unified tokenizers combine both, but encoding them within a single feature space can cause interference, and existing methods typically align acoustic features to fixed targets from a frozen semantic teacher. We propose Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization (BiSAT), a unified framework with separate acoustic and semantic branches coupled by a shared-index mechanism. During training, each branch has its own encoder, codebook, and decoder, and at every frame a shared index minimizes the combined quantization error across both branches. BiSAT thus learns acoustic and semantic representations in separate continuous spaces while producing a single discrete code stream, jointly optimizing both encoders without fixed semantic teachers. Built on BiSAT, BiSAT-TTS pairs an autoregressive text-speech LM with a conditional flow-matching acoustic decoder for zero-shot text-to-speech. Reconstruction, frozen-code understanding, and diagnostic analyses show that BiSAT preserves accessible linguistic and acoustic structure in a low-bitrate single stream, generalizes strongly to in-thewild and out-of-domain speech, and learns complementary paired codebooks. BiSAT-TTS matches or surpasses state-of-the-art speech LM-based TTS baselines with less training data, demonstrating that accessible code structure, not reconstruction quality alone, benefits autoregressive speech modeling. The audio demos are available at https://seekmind-lab.github.io/bisat-demo.

sections.content: Yixian Lu*, Lijun Wang*, Graduate Student Member, IEEE, and Shogo Okada, Member, IEEE AbstractSpeech language models (LMs) generate speech as sequences of discrete tokens, requiring tokenizers that preserve both acoustic detail and linguistic content at low bitrate. The audio demos are available at https://seekmind-lab.github.io/bisat-demo. Index TermsSpeech Tokenization, Zero-shot Text-to-Speech Synthesis, Text-Speech Language Model, Conditional Flow Matching. I. INTRODUCTION PEECH language models (LMs) generate speech as sequences of discrete tokens, enabling text-to-speech (TTS) systems to adopt large language model (LLM) architectures and training recipes for scalable sequence modeling [1][3]. In particular, autoregressive (AR) speech LMs determine output length flexibly without explicit duration modeling, in contrast to many non-autoregressive (NAR) methods [1]. Before tokenbased LM can model speech, the continuous speech waveform must be discretized. This can be performed by quantization, such as vector quantization (VQ) [4], residual vector quantization (RVQ) [5], finite scalar quantization (FSQ) [6], and binary spherical quantization (BSQ) [7]. VQ, FSQ, and BSQ give one code per frame, whereas RVQ quantizes the residual of each stage with further codebook and produces several The authors are with the Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Nomi, Ishikawa 923-1292, Japan (e-mail: yixian.lu@jaist.ac.jp; lijun.wang@jaist.ac.jp; okada-s@jaist.ac.jp). Corresponding author. code streams. Following common usage in speech tokenization [8], we use semantic to refer to the linguistic content of speech, including phonetic and lexical information. The training objective influences what information the codes retain [4]. Speech reconstruction encourages the codes to retain acoustic information such as prosody, pitch, timbre, and speaker identity [5], [9][11], whereas speech LMs also require codes that preserve semantic content. Retaining both types of information within compact single-stream bottleneck is central trade-off in designing tokenizer for speech LM. The information retained determines what the LM must model and what the acoustic decoder can recover to resynthesize the waveform. In general, LM-based TTS uses three types of speech tokenizers that differ in how they make this trade-off. Semanticenhanced tokenizers (SETs) insert quantizer into pretrained speech understanding model [2], [12][15]. Acoustic-oriented tokenizers (AOTs) learn codes primarily through waveform or mel-spectrogram reconstruction [5], [9], [16], [17]. Unified tokenizers (UTs) combine acoustic reconstruction with semantic supervision [3], [18][22]. Semantic supervision captures linguistic content but may discard fine acoustic details needed for reconstruction. Conversely, codes learned through reconstruction preserve acoustic detail well, yet they also retain variation in timbre, prosody, and recording conditions that can weaken alignment with text and cause AR LMs to repeat or skip words [18], [23], [24]. Recent UTs combine acoustic and semantic supervision in one tokenizer, either by guiding the first RVQ layer with semantic features [18], [19], [22] or by fusing the two representations before quantization [3], [20], [21]. However, encoding acoustic detail and linguistic content within single shared or fused representation space can cause interference between the two objectives. Furthermore, these methods derive semantic supervision from pretrained or frozen encoders, so the semantic targets remain fixed during tokenizer training. Finally, most AOTs and UTs reconstruct waveforms with adversarial training (AT), since regression losses alone yield over-smoothed speech at low bitrates [5], [9]. Because an adversarial discriminator evaluates naturalness rather than code faithfulness, co-trained waveform decoder can synthesize details absent from the codes, decoupling reconstruction quality from structured semantic patterns [3], [9], [17], [18], as discussed in Section II-A. These limitations motivate us to design low-bitrate singlestream tokenizer at low frame rate that learns acoustic and semantic representations in separate continuous spaces while jointly optimizing both branches without fixed semantic teachers. TokenFlow [25] showed in image tokenization that separate semantic and pixel-level codebooks linked by shared indices can support both understanding and generation. Motivated by this shared-index principle, we propose Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization (BiSAT). During training, BiSAT: BIDIRECTIONALLY ALIGNED SEMANTIC-ACOUSTIC TOKENIZATION 2 BiSAT uses separate acoustic and semantic branches, each with its own encoder, codebook, and decoder. The acoustic branch reconstructs mel spectrograms without adversarial training, and the semantic branch is trained with connectionist temporal classification (CTC). Waveform synthesis is deferred to separate acoustic decoder and vocoder during TTS, so the tokenizer codes are shaped solely by mel reconstruction and CTC supervision. At each frame, shared-index vector quantizer selects single index by minimizing the weighted sum of squared Euclidean distances across both branches. This design offers two key advantages. First, under finite discrete bottleneck [26], [27], keeping the encoders, codebooks, and training decoders in separate continuous spaces is intended to reduce potential interference between acoustic reconstruction and semantic recognition, while allowing each branch to learn task-specific representations. Second, unlike approaches that align acoustic features to fixed semantic teacher targets, BiSAT jointly optimizes both encoders. Since the shared index depends on both branches, updates to either encoder influence the quantization assignments of both branches. We refer to this coupled optimization mechanism as bidirectional alignment. We evaluate whether the resulting single code stream retains information useful for both linguistic and acoustic downstream tasks. We evaluate BiSAT on speech reconstruction from codes and on SUPERB and ML-SUPERB understanding probes [28], [29] across linguistic, speaker, and paralinguistic tasks to verify its effectiveness in preserving accessible semantic content and acoustic detail for speech LMs. We also analyze the paired codebooks and evaluate zero-shot TTS with BiSAT-TTS, combining an AR text-speech LM, reference-conditioned flow-matching acoustic decoder, and pretrained vocoder. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: 1) We propose BiSAT, unified speech tokenization framework that learns separate continuous acoustic and semantic representations while coupling index assignment across paired codebooks to produce single low-bitrate code stream. 2) We develop BiSAT-TTS, zero-shot TTS system that combines an AR text-speech LM with conditional flow-matching acoustic decoder using BiSAT tokens. 3) We provide comprehensive evaluation of BiSAT across speech reconstruction, downstream understanding, diagnostic analysis, and zero-shot TTS, showing competitive or superior performance across multiple benchmarks and validating the effectiveness of the overall framework. The rest of the manuscript is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work. Section III describes BiSAT and BiSATTTS. Section IV details experiments. Section concludes this work and Section VI discusses limitations and future work. II. RELATED WORK A. Speech Tokenization for Speech Language Modeling 1) Semantic-Enhanced Tokenizers: SETs insert quantization modules into pretrained speech understanding models. The CosyVoice series [2], [12], [13] quantizes intermediate representations of an understanding model, progressing from VQ with automatic speech recognition (ASR) supervision to FSQ and, in CosyVoice 3, multi-task supervision with ASR, language identification, emotion recognition, audio event detection, and speaker analysis. Spark-TTS [14] combines frame-level semantic tokens with fixed-length global tokens for utterance-level properties, and Qwen3-TTS [15] uses 25 Hz single-codebook tokenizer that emphasizes semantic content. The CosyVoice tokenizers are trained only with understanding tasks, so their tokens carry little of the acoustic detail needed for reconstruction. Flow-based [2], [13] or generative adversarial network (GAN) decoders [14] are thus employed to recover this detail from additional conditioning, which may demand more data and larger decoder capacity. 2) Acoustic-Oriented Tokenizers: AOTs learn codes through reconstruction. RVQ codecs such as EnCodec [9] add residual quantization layers to recover finer acoustic detail, but serializing multiple code streams into one sequence significantly increases the sequence length for AR modeling. The VALLE series [1], [23] therefore predicts the first stream with an AR LM and the residual streams with parallel NAR model. VoiceCraft and VoiceStar [30], [31] predict all streams in one AR LM through delayed codebook pattern, and CLaM-TTS [32] models probabilistic RVQ latents. WavTokenizer [17] and FocalCodec [16] reduce the sequence burden for language modeling by producing single code stream at low bitrate. We also adopt single low-bitrate code stream at low frame rate for efficient AR language modeling without predicting additional residual streams. These AOTs receive no explicit semantic supervision, so the LM must infer linguistic structure from acoustically grounded tokens, which can cause repetitions, skipped words, and nonterminating sequences [23], [24], [33]. Another problem comes from coupling tokenization with waveform reconstruction. Most of these codecs reconstruct waveforms with AT, since regression losses alone produce over-smoothed speech at low bitrates [5], [9]. The discriminator judges whether the output sounds natural, not whether it matches the input. The decoder can thus synthesize details that the codes do not contain, and the adversarial objective puts no direct pressure on the codes to form structured semantic patterns. This makes language modeling harder and demands more data, model capacity, and computation. These observations motivate us to decouple tokenization from waveform reconstruction and to supervise the tokenizer with semantic content directly. 3) Unified Tokenizers: UTs combine semantic supervision with acoustic reconstruction. SpeechTokenizer [18] and Mimi [19] guide the first RVQ layer with self-supervised learning (SSL) features from HuBERT or WavLM, while later layers encode the residual acoustic information. LM-SPT [22] reconstructs speech from its semantic tokens and matches features of the original and reconstructed speech extracted by frozen speech encoder. In these RVQ designs, the first layer must represent linguistic content while providing the acoustic approximation refined by later layers, which makes the two objectives hard to balance [18], [19], [22], [34]. XYTokenizer [20] and the X-Codec series [3], [21] instead fuse the outputs of acoustic and semantic encoders before quantization. X-Codec2 quantizes the fused features with single FSQ codebook, which allows LLaSA [3] to use one AR LM. In fusion designs, encoding acoustic detail and linguistic content BiSAT: BIDIRECTIONALLY ALIGNED SEMANTIC-ACOUSTIC TOKENIZATION within single fused representation can cause interference between the two objectives during training [20]. These methods also derive semantic supervision from pretrained or frozen speech encoders, namely teacher features [3], [18], [19], [21] or frozen encoder [20], [22], so the semantic targets remain fixed during tokenizer training. Finally, UTs couple tokenization with adversarial waveform reconstruction as in AOTs, allowing reconstruction to rely on co-trained decoders without ensuring generalizable semantic code patterns. In image tokenization, TokenFlow [25] uses separate semantic and pixel-level codebooks linked by shared indices for understanding and generation. Inspired by this design, BiSAT jointly updates acoustic and semantic encoders with separate codebooks and determines their shared discrete indices from both representations. waveform and := (y1, . . . , yU ) is its tokenized transcript. Zero-shot TTS Systems Zero-shot TTS systems include NAR, AR, continuous AR, and discrete diffusion models. NAR systems generate all frames in parallel, including flowand VAE-based models with monotonic alignment search or explicit duration modeling [35][37], latent diffusion models [10], [38], and flow-matching models that learn alignment without supervision [39], [40]. Continuous AR models predict continuous acoustic features directly, which avoids quantization error but can suffer from oversmoothing and unstable sequential generation [41], [42]. Discrete diffusion models instead generate token sequences through iterative denoising [43]. Discrete AR text-speech LMs generate speech tokens sequentially without explicit duration control. While RVQ-based systems require multi-stage or parallel prediction scheme [1], [23], [32], single-stream VQ or FSQ tokenizers allow LM [2], [3], [12], [14]. BiSAT-TTS follows this single-stream AR approach. C. Acoustic-Semantic Representation Alignment In speech, representation-level alignment between acoustic signals and linguistic content has been studied through selfsupervised pretraining [44][46], joint speech-text pretraining [47], [48], and semantic regularization of generative latent spaces [49]. These methods align acoustic and linguistic information within single continuous space. BiSAT instead initializes dual encoders from shared self-supervised speech backbone [50], specializes them under separate acoustic and semantic supervision, and couples the two continuous spaces through shared-index quantization into single code stream. Shared-index Vector Quantizer (SVQ). Motivated by the shared-index principle of TokenFlow [25], we design shared-index quantization scheme using two codebooks of size Dcodebook, one for each branch, with Dcodebook = 512. By Eq. (4), the quantizer selects one shared index zt {1, . . . , K} per frame, so the frame-level discrete bottleneck remains log2 bits. This design has two key properties. (i) Separate continuous representation spaces. During training, each shared index retrieves paired acoustic and semantic entries czt,a and czt,s, which are passed to their respective decoders. Learning the two continuous spaces and codebooks separately allows each branch to develop task-specific representations without requiring acoustic detail and linguistic units to be encoded in the same continuous feature vector. At the same time, the joint distance in Eq. (4) allows frames that are similar in one branch but different in the other to be assigned to different codebook indices, partitioning the paired entries according to both acoustic and semantic structure. Together with spherical k-means initialization, EMA updates, and dead-code replacement, this yields training codebook utilization of 100% for BiSAT-32k and 99.8% for BiSAT-64k, as shown in Table II. (ii) Bidirectional alignment. The shared index zt in Eq. (4) depends on both ea,t and es,t, grouping frames under the joint acoustic and semantic distance. Mel-spectrogram reconstruction updates the acoustic encoder and CTC updates the semantic encoder, while EMA updates in Eq. (17) adapt both codebooks from the same assigned frames. Through shared-index assignment, updates in either encoder affect the quantization assignments of both branches, coupling their optimization without relying on fixed semantic teacher features [3], [18], [19], [21], [22]. Notably, the CosyVoice tokenizers are the most comparable baselines to BiSAT, as they also produce single 25 Hz code stream at similar bitrate and reconstruct speech through CFM acoustic decoder. In particular, BiSAT uses the same DiT backbone configuration as CosyVoice 3 for its CFM acoustic decoder, while using 512-d code and 192-d speaker conditions rather than 80-d projections. TTS Baselines. We compare BiSAT-TTS with zero-shot TTS systems that generate discrete speech tokens with an AR LM, using their official checkpoints and default inference settings. The baselines include CosyVoice 1, 2, and 3 [2], [12], [13], Spark-TTS [14], VoiceStar [31], and LLaSA-1B and LLaSA3B [3] built on X-Codec2. For VoiceStar, the required target duration is estimated from the speaking rate of the prompt as in [31]. Note that the acoustic decoders of the CosyVoice series and BiSAT-TTS condition on reference mel prompt and speaker embedding, whereas Spark-TTS, VoiceStar, and LLaSA synthesize waveforms from the code sequence alone. 5) Evaluation Metrics: Tokenizer Evaluation. Reconstruction and understanding assess the acoustic and semantic information retained in the codes. Reconstruction. Perceived naturalness is measured by the neural mean opinion score (MOS) predictor UTMOSv2 [80]. Speaker similarity (SIM) is the cosine similarity between speaker embeddings of the resynthesized and original speech, extracted with the WavLM-Base+ speaker verification model [46]. On LibriSpeech-PC, we measure intelligibility by the word error rate (WER) of Whisper-large-v3 [81]. CosyVoice 2, CosyVoice 3, and BiSAT reconstruct speech without mel prompt, using codes and speaker condition extracted from the target utterance. The other tokenizers decode from the codes alone. All systems reconstruct the same input utterance without separate reference utterance. For harder in-the-wild setting, we also evaluate on the crowdsourced Common Voice 27 [77] test sets of English, French, German, Mandarin, Japanese, and Korean, using the same reconstruction protocol. The English set excludes the clips and speakers used in Seed-TTS test-en. BiSAT: BIDIRECTIONALLY ALIGNED SEMANTIC-ACOUSTIC TOKENIZATION 9 For Mandarin, we compute the character error rate (CER) with Paraformer-zh. For the other languages, we use Whisper-largev3 with Whisper normalizers and report CER for Japanese and Korean and WER for English, French, and German. Understanding. We adapt the SUPERB [28] and MLSUPERB [29] protocols to discrete codes in place of continuous SSL features. For each tokenizer, we train probe on the frozen codes at the tokenizers own frame rate. The probe consists of learned code embedding table and an 8-layer, 512-dimensional Transformer encoder, followed by CTC head for recognition tasks or attentive pooling with classification head for the other tasks. All tokenizers use the same probe and training recipe for each task. The English tasks follow SUPERB. ASR in the other languages and language identification (LID) follow MLSUPERB. For English ASR, the probe is trained on LibriSpeech train-clean-100 [82]. For the other languages, we follow the monolingual ASR setting of ML-SUPERB and train separate probe for each language on 100 hours of single corpus. These are 100-hour subsets of MLS [83] for French and German, subset of WenetSpeech [84] for Mandarin, and the small subset of ReazonSpeech [85] for Japanese. We evaluate ASR only in the zero-shot out-of-domain setting, using the Common Voice [77] and FLEURS [86] test sets for each language. These corpora are not used to train the ASR probes. We train the phoneme recognition (PR) probe on LibriSpeech train-clean100 and test it on test-clean. For automatic speaker verification (ASV) and speaker identification (SID), we use VoxCeleb1 [87]. For emotion recognition (ER), shared seven-class head is trained on IEMOCAP [88], CREMA-D [89], RAVDESS [90], and the English portion of ESD [91]. It is evaluated on IEMOCAP with SUPERBs five-fold leave-one-session-out protocol. Following the multilingual LID setting of ML-SUPERB, single LID probe covers 12 languages (Mandarin, Cantonese, English, Japanese, Korean, French, German, Dutch, Italian, Polish, Portuguese, and Spanish). It is trained on FLEURS and VoxLingua107 [92] and tested on the pooled FLEURS test and VoxLingua107 development sets. ASR is reported as WER, or as CER for Mandarin and Japanese, PR as phone error rate (PER), ASV as equal error rate (EER), SID and LID as accuracy, and ER as weighted accuracy over the five folds. TTS Evaluation. We evaluate cross-sentence zero-shot TTS on LibriSpeech-PC test-clean [76], following the VALL-E protocol [1] and the evaluation settings of [40]. The prompt is different utterance from the same speaker, and the text-speech LM takes the annotated prompt transcript followed by the target text. We also evaluate the cross-sentence setting on Seed-TTS test-zh and test-en [93]. On LibriSpeech-PC, we report the WER of Whisper-large-v3 with its text normalizer, speaker similarity against the original prompt (SIM-o) computed with the WavLM-Base+ speaker verification model [46], UTMOSv2 for perceived naturalness, and NISQA [94] for overall speech quality. On Seed-TTS, we report SIM-o using the official WavLM-Large ECAPA-TDNN model, with the WER of Whisper-large-v3 on test-en, the CER of Paraformer-zh [95] on test-zh, and UTMOSv2 and NISQA on both sets. We average utterance-level scores over three seeds. For WER and CER, we assign empty clips an error rate of 100% and leave error rates for nonempty clips uncapped. For similarity and quality metrics, we average scores over scorable clips. The failure rate (Fail) is the percentage of clips across all evaluated sets that are empty or have WER or CER of at least 100%. For test-en, we use the Whisper normalizer instead of that of the Seed-TTS toolkit for more accurate results, since it excludes differences that exist only in the written form but are pronounced identically, such as number formats. B. Experimental Results 1) Tokenizer Evaluation: Reconstruction. Table II shows that BiSAT preserves both intelligibility and speaker fidelity at low bitrate without adversarial waveform training. Among tokenizers at comparable bitrates, BiSAT achieves the strongest intelligibility and speaker similarity on LibriSpeech-PC while trailing only CosyVoice 2 in UTMOSv2. Despite the joint contribution of the discrete codes and the target speaker condition to SIM for BiSAT and the CosyVoice tokenizers, BiSAT-32k also leads on SID and ASV in Table III, which isolate the effect of the speaker condition and show that the codes themselves retain strong speaker information. Moreover, BiSATs margin over CosyVoice 3 rises from 0.11% on clean LibriSpeech-PC to 0.4-1.7% across English, French, German, and Korean on the in-the-wild Common Voice 27 sets despite using less than quarter of CosyVoice 3s training data, with Japanese as the only exception. These results indicate that BiSATs bidirectional alignment produces codes that generalize better across varied accents, microphones, and background noise than purely semantic or feature-fusion tokenization. Among the codecs that resynthesize the waveform from the codes alone using adversarial training, WavTokenizer has UTMOSv2 close to the ground truth but about three times the WER of FocalCodec. Natural-sounding output thus does not ensure that the content is preserved, as discussed in Section II-A2. X-Codec2 achieves reconstruction WER close to BiSAT, yet the probes trained on its codes perform substantially worse on speech and phoneme recognition in Table III, showing that low reconstruction error alone does not mean linguistic information is readily accessible from the codes. FocalCodec shows the opposite pattern, with higher SID accuracy than the SETs but more recognition errors. As shown in Table IV, BiSAT-TTS achieves lower WER, CER, and Fail rates than all baselines, far below Spark-TTS and LLaSA. Against CosyVoice 3, under the same 0.5B LM scale, 25 Hz frame rate, and DiT backbone, BiSAT-TTS achieves much lower error rates on every set with roughly one-eighth of its 1 Mhour training set [13], widening the LibriSpeech-PC WER margin from 0.11 points in reconstruction to 0.23 points in TTS. Comparing Tables II, III, and IV clarifies how code structure affects AR modeling, notably on X-Codec2. Although X-Codec2 nears BiSAT in LibriSpeech-PC reconstruction WER (2.27% vs. 2.15%) at over twice the bitrate, its weak ASR, PR, and SID probes (Table III) show that AT-based reconstruction can achieve low error without cleanly structured codes. Consequently, both LLaSA-1B and LLaSA-3B still have much higher error and Fail rates than BiSAT-TTS on every set despite up to 6 the LM scale and twice the training data. Strong reconstruction can thus mask weakly structured codes that hinder AR generation, whereas BiSATs lower error and Fail rates alongside Table IIIs results indicate that preserving accessible semantic and acoustic structure yields code representations better suited for AR speech modeling. Speaker Similarity. BiSAT-TTS closely approaches CosyVoice 3s SIM-o on LibriSpeech-PC and trails only CosyVoice 3 on Seed-TTS test-en. The larger gap to CosyVoice 2 and 3 on test-zh may reflect their larger Mandarin training sets rather than tokenizer bottleneck, consistent with BiSATs leading SID and ASV scores in Table III. Perceived Naturalness and Speech Quality. Relative to CosyVoice 3, BiSAT-TTS achieves comparable UTMOSv2 2https://github.com/mmorise/World 3https://montreal-forced-aligner.readthedocs.io scores on all three sets, whereas CosyVoice 2 and Spark-TTS score highest. Unlike LLaSA and Spark-TTS, which use AT waveform decoders [3], [14], BiSAT-TTS and CosyVoice condition flow-matching decoders on reference mel prompts. Because prompt-conditioned flow matching tends to preserve prompt acoustics and background noise [101], reference-free UTMOSv2 scores can be lower on in-the-wild Seed-TTS prompts than for AT decoders. On NISQA, which evaluates overall quality across noisiness, coloration, discontinuity, and loudness [94], both BiSAT-TTS variants still outperform CosyVoice 3, Spark-TTS, and both LLaSA models on all three sets. CosyVoice 2s strong scores on both metrics may also reflect its convolutional Transformer U-Net decoder rather than the DiT in CosyVoice 3 and BiSAT [2], [13]. Overall, BiSAT balances intelligibility, speaker similarity, naturalness, and speech quality well in practice. 4) Codebook Size Ablation: Larger codebooks increase capacity but risk VQ collapse and expand the AR output and vocabulary, making next-token prediction harder typically demanding larger models and more training data. Comparing BiSAT-32k (K = 32768, 375 bps) and BiSAT-64k (K = 65536, 400 bps) across Tables II and IV, maintaining 99.8% training utilization at 64 for 6.7% higher bitrate shows that shared-index assignment across separate continuous spaces, together with spherical k-means initialization, EMA updates, and dead-code replacement, prevents collapse even in large paired vocabulary. In Table II, BiSAT-64k slightly improves LibriSpeech-PC UTMOSv2 scores at comparable WER and SIM while modestly lowering WER and CER on most Common Voice 27 sets except Japanese, indicating that 32 suffices for clean speech whereas 64 improves robustness on noisier in-the-wild speech. PolyShift edges out cosine on most BiSAT-32k reconstruction sets, while both schedules perform comparably at 64 and in TTS. In Table IV, BiSAT-TTS-64k lowers Seed-TTS WER/CER, raises Seed-TTS UTMOSv2, and improves NISQA across all three sets, with comparable LibriSpeech-PC WER and nearly unchanged SIM-o. Since LM output-head size and sampling settings also differ, this reflects an end-to-end trade-off while showing that BiSAT scales effectively to 64 codebook without degrading AR modeling under the same LM scale and data. BiSAT: BIDIRECTIONALLY ALIGNED SEMANTIC-ACOUSTIC TOKENIZATION 12 V. CONCLUSION We proposed BiSAT, unified speech tokenizer that jointly optimizes separate acoustic and semantic branches into single code stream via shared-index assignment without fixed semantic teachers. Built on BiSAT, BiSAT-TTS pairs an AR text-speech LM with conditional flow-matching acoustic decoder for zero-shot TTS. Experiments across reconstruction, understanding, and diagnostic analyses show that BiSAT preserves linguistic and acoustic structure, generalizes to inthe-wild and out-of-domain speech, and learns complementary paired codebooks. In zero-shot TTS, BiSAT-TTS matches or surpasses state-of-the-art AR baselines with less training data. Finally, these results show that reconstruction metrics alone do not capture accessible structure for AR language modeling, making frozen-code understanding probes essential complementary indicators of token quality. VI. LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK Due to our limited training budget, we could not validate BiSAT at larger scale, especially for the tokenizer, where both encoders are initialized from the English-pretrained NeMo SSL Conformer rather than larger multilingual encoder. Combined with much less Mandarin and Japanese training data [13], this may limit performance on those languages compared with CosyVoice 3, and scaling the text-speech LM also remains to be studied. Unlike end-to-end waveform codecs such as X-Codec2 that reconstruct waveforms directly from codes alone, BiSAT relies on separate speaker-conditioned flow-matching decoder and vocoder. Despite our diagnostic analysis and codebook-size ablation, this study evaluates BiSAT as whole without controlled full-scale ablations of its individual architectural components. In future work, we plan to isolate these component contributions, explore direct end-to-end waveform reconstruction, and extend BiSAT to code-based RL post-training and speech-to-speech LMs.
